entities.name: Albert Rhys Williams
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Albert Rhys Williams (1883–1962) was an American Congregationalist minister, journalist, and ardent supporter of the Russian Revolution who became one of the most prominent American fellow-travellers of the early Soviet period. Born in Woodstock, Connecticut, he was ordained a Congregationalist minister and worked as a parish pastor before his journalistic career took him to Russia in 1917, where he witnessed the October Revolution alongside John Reed.

Williams remained in Russia through the Revolution and Civil War, becoming one of a small group of American eyewitnesses to the Bolshevik seizure of power. His 1921 book 'Through the Russian Revolution' was an enthusiastic account of the revolutionary process from the perspective of a sympathiser. Like John Reed's 'Ten Days That Shook the World,' his work presented the Bolshevik Revolution as a heroic liberation movement, influencing American radical opinion for decades.

As an ordained minister who embraced revolutionary socialism, Williams represented a distinctive strain of American religious radicalism that found in Bolshevism a secular analogue to Christian redemption. His career illustrates the complex intersection of Protestant social gospel theology, American progressive politics, and international revolutionary sympathy in the early twentieth century. He continued to advocate for the Soviet Union through the 1930s and 1940s, outlasting many fellow-travellers who eventually broke with Moscow.
